scope: planned variation between lessons, never random on reopen

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! Your gate is different now. Please go to gate eight, not gate six. It’s next to the café. You have time for some water. Keep your passport with you. I’m near the gate. See you there!
photo: An airport terminal, shared as context for the gate change
changes.greeting: The gate has changed — here’s the terminal

changes.name: Evelyn
changes.sourceAudioText: Hello, Ana. This is reception. Someone can come to your room at seven this evening, not six. We have two towels for you here. You can collect them now, or we can bring them at seven. Please tell us what you need. Thank you!
changes.greeting: Reception has a new time for you

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! Let’s meet at the park, not the café. Start at the hotel and go straight. Turn right at the second street. The park is at the end, after the market. I’m near the trees. See you in ten minutes!
photo: A street scene, shared as context for the route to the park
changes.greeting: Here’s the area near our meeting point

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! Can you order something for me? I’d like some tea and a piece of cake, please. No milk in the tea. I’m outside the café, near the door. I have six dollars. Thank you! I’ll see you in a minute.
changes.greeting: Here’s a short café-ordering clip for our practice

changes.name: Ruby
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! Thank you for looking for my gift. I like the green T-shirt. Medium is right for me. I don’t need a jacket. Twelve dollars is OK. Can you bring the T-shirt on Friday? We can meet at the café. Thank you!
changes.greeting: I found the T-shirt I’d like

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! It’s raining near the park now. Let’s go to the museum today. Meet me at the museum entrance at ten, not at the station. We can take the bus. Bring your ticket. There’s a café inside. See you at ten!
changes.greeting: It’s raining — shall we change our plan?

changes.name: Niamh
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! You asked about my Sunday. I didn’t visit the museum in the end. The weather was beautiful, so I went to the beach instead. I walked for an hour and took some photos. Then I had lunch with a friend. It was a quiet afternoon, but I really enjoyed it. What did you do?
changes.greeting: Here’s what I ended up doing on Sunday

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Leo just called me. He was driving to the café when he got stuck in traffic. There’s a lot of traffic near the station, so he’s running late too. He thinks he can be here at one thirty. He’s fine, and he says we should order our food now. Shall we get a table?
changes.greeting: I’ve heard from Leo about the traffic

changes.lessonTitle: Are you doing anything on Saturday?
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! I checked the food festival. It opens at eleven on Sunday, not ten. Would eleven thirty work for you? We could meet at the main entrance and have lunch there. I’m still free in the afternoon. If Sunday is difficult, the festival is also open on Saturday until six. What do you think?
changes.greeting: This clip gave me another idea for making plans

changes.name: Owen
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! A quick update about the move: the lift isn’t working this afternoon. We have to take the stairs. The heavy box can stay downstairs for now, but I need help carrying the small bags. Could you come at three? I’m still going to paint tomorrow, so there’s no need to bring paint today. Thank you!
changes.greeting: One thing has changed for the move

changes.name: Evelyn
changes.sourceAudioText: Hello, Ana. This is a message about your appointment at the Green Clinic. The time is now four o’clock this afternoon, not three. The address is the same. Please come to reception ten minutes before your appointment. You don’t need to reply if four is OK. If you need another time, please call reception. Thank you.
changes.greeting: A message about your clinic appointment

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! There’s a temporary change this weekend. The pool closes at six, not eight, because of cleaning. The grill booking is still fine, and you can use the chairs. If your friends want to swim, they should come before six. Could you tell them about the earlier closing time? Everything goes back to normal on Monday.
changes.greeting: I checked this weekend’s opening times

changes.lessonTitle: Have you ever been to Lisbon?
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! A quick update from Lisbon. I’ve tried a pastel de nata now, and I loved it. I had one at a small café this morning. I haven’t visited the aquarium yet. I’m thinking of going tomorrow, but I haven’t booked a ticket. Have you ever been? I’d love to know what you thought of it before I decide.
changes.greeting: A little update from Lisbon

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! Here’s the update for our fictional profile. I moved to Porto in 2023, and I’ve lived here since then. I started the photography group in 2025, and I still go on Sundays. I haven’t changed jobs, but I’ve finished an online course. I’m really enjoying the city now. What would you like to ask about my new routine?
changes.greeting: I’ve checked the details for our practice profile

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! I asked about apartment A. There’s a busy road outside, and it can be noisy at night. The price, two beds and distance are the same. Apartment B is on a quiet street. I still want my own bed, but I also need to sleep well. Does this change your choice? We could ask A about a quieter room before we book.
photo: The apartment visit, shared as context for the noise update
changes.greeting: Here’s the apartment visit we talked about

changes.name: Priya
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! The forecast says it will rain on Sunday morning. Let’s use our backup plan. If it rains, we’ll go straight to the museum, and we’ll have lunch inside. We can still take the nine o’clock bus. If that bus is late, let’s wait for the nine thirty one rather than walk in the rain. Does that work for you?
changes.greeting: Let’s use our rainy-day plan

changes.pageTitle: A friend can only come on Saturday
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! I heard from our friends. One of them can’t come on Friday, but everyone is free on Saturday at eight. We still need step-free access, and twenty dollars each is OK. Could you change the date before you book? The Garden Table has a table on Saturday. Let me know what you decide, and I’ll send the invitation.
changes.greeting: I’ve checked when everyone can come

changes.lessonTitle: There used to be a cinema here
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana! I checked another change on our example map. There used to be a factory beside the square. It’s an apartment block now, with a small garden in front. The playground is still in the same place. A former resident told me he used to work at the factory, so he misses it, even though he likes the cleaner street. Would you show him what has changed and ask which part he remembers best?
changes.greeting: I noticed another change near the square

changes.name: Ruby
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I’ve checked what happened at the entrance in our concert story. They couldn’t get in immediately because one person had left their wristband at home. The entrance was still open at eight twenty, so closing time wasn’t the problem. The help desk could issue a replacement if they showed the digital ticket. They eventually got in, but the opening act had already finished. Could you explain the sequence to someone who thinks they were turned away because they arrived late?
changes.greeting: I found out what happened at the concert entrance

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Reception has spoken to a caller about the backpack. The caller described a black notebook with a silver star and a red fish key ring, without being told those details first. Both descriptions match the objects in our example. That makes the claim more plausible, but reception still needs to follow its collection procedure. Could you explain why the matching details are stronger evidence than simply having a charger, and say what still needs to be checked?
changes.greeting: Someone has called about the backpack

changes.lessonTitle: He said he’d come on Thursday
changes.name: Owen
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I’ve had another call about the repair. He said he couldn’t come on Thursday after all and would come on Friday at eleven instead. He still asked us to leave the spare key at reception. He also said the visit might take longer than an hour if the tap needs replacing. Could you pass that on to the building manager and check that the new time has been understood? The earlier Thursday booking should be removed from the diary.
changes.greeting: The repair person has changed the appointment

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I’m most concerned about having time for an afternoon course. A higher salary would be welcome, but it isn’t the main reason I’m thinking of changing jobs. I’d accept a longer commute on some days if the flexible hours were real. Before I choose offer B, could you help me decide what to ask the employer? They haven’t confirmed whether I can keep my afternoons free. I’d like to check that before accepting.
changes.greeting: I’ve been thinking about what matters most to me

changes.lessonTitle: I should have taken the direct flight
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. There’s still a flight available this evening. It leaves at six and gets in at eight thirty, but the desk hasn’t confirmed a seat yet. The direct flight tomorrow morning would arrive at ten and costs more. The traveller needs to be there by nine tomorrow, so the evening option could work if a seat is confirmed. Could you explain the two choices and what must be checked? A refund and insurance payment have not been confirmed.
changes.greeting: There’s still a flight we could ask about

changes.lessonTitle: I’m getting used to the cold
changes.name: Niamh
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Taking the bus is much easier now. I’m used to checking the timetable before I leave, so I haven’t missed the last bus again. The cold is still difficult, especially deciding what to wear when the weather changes during the day. I’ve joined a weekly group, but I sometimes feel homesick in the evenings. It isn’t all wonderful or all terrible! What helped you get used to a different routine? I’d really like to hear your experience.
changes.greeting: I’m getting used to some things here

changes.pageTitle: A similar bike has been found
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. There’s an update about the bicycle report. A blue bike with a black basket has been found near the station. The yellow sticker hasn’t been confirmed, and the serial number hasn’t been checked yet. It may be the missing bike, but it hasn’t been identified as yours. Reception will contact you when the identifying details have been compared. Could you tell the other person what has actually been confirmed, and what you still need to ask?
photo: A bicycle scene, shared as context for the missing-bike update
changes.greeting: Here’s a bike picture to go with the update

changes.lessonTitle: Could you tell me where it is?
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. There’s a room change for the eleven thirty talk. It’s now in room four, not room two. The ten o’clock tour still starts at reception. The message doesn’t say whether room four has step-free access, and one person in our group needs it. Could you check that before we leave the ground floor? The entrance fee still includes the standard tour; we haven’t booked the extra workshop.
changes.greeting: Here’s a useful way to ask for information politely

changes.lessonTitle: The woman who’s dancing with Leo
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Before you introduce me at our example celebration, could you help me find Alex? Alex is the host, the person in the green shirt standing by the drinks table. I don’t mean Nina, who organised the music and is near the dance floor. The speech is almost finished, so we can go over afterwards. Please introduce me using the facts on Alex’s card rather than guessing a job or a family relationship.
changes.greeting: Could you help me find the host?

changes.pageTitle: Hybrid works, but the schedule doesn’t
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Working at home helps me concentrate, and two office days make it easier to speak to the team. However, the office days have been changing at short notice, so planning childcare and travel has become difficult. I don’t want to stop seeing colleagues. I’d like to keep the benefit but make the schedule more predictable. What would you suggest I ask the team to agree on? I don’t think one routine has to be best for everyone.
changes.greeting: Hybrid working helps, but the schedule is a problem

changes.lessonTitle: By Friday I’ll have finished it
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. The draft is ready, but the review has moved from Wednesday to Thursday afternoon. The final changes still need roughly one working day after we receive the comments. That means we shouldn’t promise the final pack for Friday morning. We can have a short welcome sheet ready by ten, while the full pack is still being checked. Could you ask whether that would cover the volunteers’ immediate needs? If it does, we can agree a later handover for the complete version rather than quietly sending an unchecked draft. We also need to make clear that a new section would require another estimate.
changes.greeting: The review date has changed again

changes.lessonTitle: If I hadn’t gone to Toronto
changes.name: Priya
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. There’s one more detail about that short course. The unexpected benefit wasn’t a job offer. The person met someone who later invited them to help with a community project. They still collaborate now, and that work has made it easier to explain their skills to other people. If they hadn’t gone to Toronto, that particular collaboration might not exist today. But it would be too strong to say they’d have no opportunities at all. Could you explain the present consequence and then describe a plausible alternative, making clear which part is a fact and which part is only a possibility?
changes.greeting: There was an unexpected benefit from that course

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. The neighbour has confirmed that she used the spare key at five to water the plants. She says she moved the plant away from the closed window before leaving. That supports the explanation of an authorised visit. She doesn’t recognise the receipt from five twenty, though, so we still don’t know who left it or when it came into the flat. Could you update the explanation without making the receipt fit by inventing another visit? We have confirmation for the key and the plant, but only an unresolved clue for the receipt.
changes.greeting: I checked what the message actually means

changes.lessonTitle: We needn’t have paid in advance
changes.name: Evelyn
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Reception checked the booking and agrees that breakfast was already included in the room price. They can return the twenty-dollar breakfast charge if we provide the receipt reference; it may take three business days. The fifty-dollar deposit is different. It will be assessed after the room check at departure, so it hasn’t been approved for return yet. Could you explain which amount we can request now and which condition still applies to the deposit? We don’t need to give any bank details in this practice conversation.
changes.greeting: The hotel has checked our booking

changes.lessonTitle: I need to get the screen fixed
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. The new screen has been fitted, but the phone is still being tested. The shop now expects collection on Saturday at five, one day later than planned. They do have a temporary phone available from Friday at four, free of charge, to be returned when you collect yours. That may cover the trip, but you’d need to check that it supports what you need and arrange your own account access. Could you respond to the shop, confirm the revised collection time and ask one relevant question about the temporary phone? The repair quote remains eighty dollars.
changes.greeting: I have another detail for the decision

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I want to clarify the dinner message. I suggested Saturday because it seemed convenient; I didn’t insist on that date or promise that everyone would pay in advance. I’m happy to consider another evening. The host said they would book only after checking availability, and one guest still wants to see the cancellation conditions before paying anything. Could you pass that on without making me sound more definite than I was? A useful summary would say what was suggested, what was actually promised and what is still unresolved.
changes.greeting: Here’s what I found out about the situation

changes.lessonTitle: The apartment, which has a balcony
changes.pageTitle: The advertised rent wasn’t the total
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. The landlord has confirmed that apartment C has a maintenance fee of one hundred and fifty dollars a month, on top of the nine hundred and fifty rent. That takes the total to eleven hundred, above the profile’s firm thousand-dollar limit. The balcony is still appealing, but it doesn’t remove the budget constraint. A and B haven’t changed. Could you revise the recommendation, explain which detail changes it and ask which of the remaining trade-offs matters more? We still need to see whether the work corner in A is comfortable enough for two home-working days a week.
changes.greeting: There’s one condition we still need to check

changes.lessonTitle: I don’t remember locking the door
changes.name: Ruby
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I’ve checked the flat. The door is locked, the stove is off, and the iron is unplugged. The window was open, so I’ve closed it as you asked. I haven’t watered the plants yet because you wanted to decide the timing first. Would you like me to water them today or come back on Saturday? I can do either. Please send that one instruction when you have a moment. Everything else on the list has been checked, so there’s no need to ask me to repeat the whole routine.
changes.greeting: I’ve checked the flat — just one question left

changes.lessonTitle: What I need is a quiet room
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Reception has offered a room on the quiet side of the building, away from the lift. It will be ready at nine this evening. They can help move the bags, and there is no extra room charge. That addresses the location of the noise, but we still need to confirm whether any maintenance work is planned nearby tonight. You have an early presentation, so the timing matters too. Would you accept the offer, subject to that check, or ask for another arrangement? Could you make clear which part meets the need and which detail is still unresolved?
changes.greeting: I have a detail that changes our next step

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. One group member likes the shorter meeting but is worried about asking questions after the live discussion. They can’t always join at the same time, and they don’t want their questions to disappear in a long message thread. They suggest a separate question channel, with a named person checking it each study day. Could you revise the proposal without bringing back the full sixty-minute status round? Keep its purpose—more useful time—and explain what you would change so people can still get an answer. We should agree how to review the trial before calling it a success.
changes.greeting: Here’s an update on what we discussed

changes.lessonTitle: Should phones be banned at school?
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. There’s a case our draft policy hasn’t addressed. A learner uses a phone to read material aloud and communicate when speaking is difficult. Asking for permission publicly every lesson would draw attention to private information and could delay participation. The learner isn’t asking to use social media. Could you reconsider how the exception works, rather than treating this as a choice between no rules and unlimited phone use? A private agreement, clear permitted use and a way to review problems might be worth discussing. The main classroom concern remains repeated social-message checking, so we still need a rule that addresses that specific problem.
changes.greeting: I’ve thought about the options a little more

changes.pageTitle: A warning existed, but who owned it?
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I found the missing message record. A warning that the sound test was incomplete was sent before the planned opening time, but it went to a shared group without a named person responsible for responding. There’s no acknowledgement in the record. That makes a communication failure more plausible than simply saying nobody noticed a problem. It still doesn’t establish whether enough testing time had been scheduled, or whether a recipient read the warning and chose not to act. Could you revise the review to reflect that distinction? I’d like one preventive action linked to what we can actually establish, rather than a general instruction to be more careful. If you use “Had we known”, please make clear whose knowledge you mean.
changes.greeting: There’s a useful distinction in the update

changes.lessonTitle: The company is said to be…
changes.pageTitle: No reopening date has been set
changes.name: Owen
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. The source has clarified the café notice. The dining area is closing for renovation, and delivery will continue, but a reopening date has not been set. The earlier post’s claim of permanent closure is not supported by the official notice. Could you revise the update with that attribution intact? Please don’t replace the false certainty with a confident reopening date. If people need to plan a visit, the useful next step is to check the café’s own updates rather than repeat the same unverified post. We can explain what the notice confirms and what it leaves open without implying that every part of the original rumour has been investigated independently.
changes.greeting: Here’s another example of checking a claim before passing it on

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I can make the regular family call before ten thirty, using the smaller room and headphones. I’m willing to keep the shared room quiet after nine, provided we allow a brief exception for an urgent call and I message you if that happens. I’m not asking for unlimited late calls; I just don’t want us to treat an emergency as a broken routine agreement. Could you tell me whether that protects the concentration time you need? If the sound still carries, we can review the room arrangement rather than turn it into a judgement about either person’s consideration for others.
changes.greeting: I’d like to clarify what I’m asking for

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I found the ending of the scarf story. The café staff discovered it on the chair where the traveller had left a coat earlier. A photograph taken before departure showed the scarf there already, so it hadn’t disappeared on the train at all. The staff kept it behind the counter, and the traveller collected it later. What made the ending surprising wasn’t a dramatic theft or a stranger’s secret plan. It was the discovery that the initial timeline was wrong. Could you retell it so I first understand the worried expectation, then see why that photograph changes the explanation? You can use a simple sentence for the revelation; an inverted phrase is only useful if it gives the moment the emphasis you want.
photo: The scarf on the café chair before departure
changes.greeting: I found the photograph from before the train journey

changes.lessonTitle: The more I think about it…
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. Course A has changed its live session from Wednesday to Tuesday, still seven to nine. The person on our brief has a regular Tuesday commitment and cannot attend live then. The provider also says the practical feedback is only given during that live class, not on a recording afterwards. The price and eight-week length are unchanged. This turns attendance from a flexible preference into a serious constraint. Course B’s Friday check-in still fits, but we should confirm whether its feedback covers the person’s project before accepting the higher cost. Could you explain how the balance has changed rather than simply saying the more expensive course is now better? There may also be a later run of A worth asking about.
changes.greeting: One more detail before we draw a conclusion

changes.name: Priya
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. The supplier has confirmed that the lower quote of four thousand eight hundred is available on the thirteenth of December. The budget limit remains five thousand. That resolves the pending supplier date, but it doesn’t automatically confirm the team’s availability or authorise the spending. Could you update both briefings? The funding person now has a costed option to review; the rota organiser can ask who is available for that date. Please preserve the distinction between a supplier confirmation and our own final event confirmation. We don’t need to repeat the colour discussion or every abandoned suggestion. A useful summary gives the decision, its reason and the next action for this particular recipient.
changes.greeting: The supplier has confirmed the date and price

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I’ve thought about the group-session proposal. I can accept two live sessions a month instead of four, and I’m happy to try short written updates between them. I still need the dates confirmed at least seven days ahead; reducing the frequency doesn’t remove that planning need. Could we treat the two-session arrangement as a four-week trial and review whether the updates cover the gaps? We seem to agree on regular contact and a trial. The sticking point is not willingness to participate, but the notice required to make participation feasible. Please could you confirm that part explicitly before we tell the group the whole proposal has been accepted?
changes.greeting: I checked what is possible and what isn’t

changes.pageTitle: Total capacity is not all-day coverage
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. There’s a limitation in the transport projection. The extra service is confirmed, but it only runs in the morning peak. The demand we’re discussing includes afternoon trips as well. So the added total capacity cannot automatically be treated as coverage for every part of the day. That doesn’t prove demand will keep rising at the same rate, or that the whole plan will fail. It does mean we should qualify the assumption that the extra service removes the problem. Could you revise the recommendation with that distinction? A useful next step would identify what afternoon information is needed and what observation would trigger another decision, rather than simply moving from “everything is solved” to “it’s bound to get worse”.
changes.greeting: There’s an update on how certain we can be

changes.lessonTitle: I’m writing to let you know…
changes.name: Niamh
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I’ve read the event update, but I’m not sure what you need from me. When you say “please acknowledge”, do you only want me to confirm I’ve seen the message, or do you need to know whether I can attend on Monday? I can send either, but they aren’t the same commitment. Could you also give the response deadline as a day and time rather than “tomorrow”? I sometimes read messages after the day they were sent. The new date, same ten o’clock start and room two are clear. It’s the requested action that needs clarification, so there’s no need to rewrite every factual detail or make the wording more elaborate.
changes.greeting: Could you clarify what you need me to confirm?

changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I think my request for a quick reply has been misunderstood. I wasn’t asking for the checked figures today. I was asking for a prompt acknowledgement and a realistic time for the complete answer. If verification takes until four tomorrow, please say that. What’s difficult is silence, followed by a rushed answer that looks final but hasn’t been checked. Could you explain both positions again so they can see the common ground? One person is protecting accuracy; the other is trying to plan around a response. A useful reformulation should make those needs visible and give an example, rather than repeat the word quick more loudly. Please check that they agree with your summary before treating it as their settled position.
changes.greeting: I’ve checked the wording of that explanation

changes.pageTitle: An ordinary user loses digital access
changes.name: Kim
changes.sourceAudioText: Hi, Ana. I wanted to add an experience to the payment-policy discussion. I normally pay by card, but last week my phone battery died while I was out. At the next place, the payment connection also stopped working for a while. I had some cash with me, but their digital-only process didn’t allow it, so I couldn’t complete the purchase then. I’m not saying that one incident proves digital payment is always unreliable. It does show that temporary loss of access can affect people who usually use it comfortably. Could your recommendation say what happens in that situation, including how staff explain the fallback without embarrassing the customer? I’d also want to know whether a transaction fee changes between the normal process and the fallback. A policy can aim for convenience while still making a specific plan for the moment the convenient route fails.
changes.greeting: There’s another perspective to consider

changes.name: Owen
changes.sourceAudioText: A quick update about our next study session. We’ll use audio only, so we won’t share screens or code. Choose one feature from your practice project. Explain what it does and who would use it. One more thing: tell me what you tested and what you still want to improve. Send me a short voice note before we meet. If you’re stuck, include the error message and one thing you’ve already tried.

changes.name: Priya
changes.sourceAudioText: For the technical interview, we’ll use a customer portal login. A customer enters an email and password. With a wrong password, the form should stay open and show a clear error. Please explain how you would investigate and test that behavior. You don’t need to prepare slides or write code during the call. Bring one real or practice project and explain your own contribution. We’ll leave time for your questions about the team, and I’ll send feedback by Friday.

retained: InfluencerRoutine Kim sends two notes before bed
noWhatsAppExpansion: TrialB1/B2 existing review slices are not expanded by this task
